body:
A dollar store that stopped charging just a dollar offers a useful way into Bain Capital Private Equity: buy a business, question its habits, and make the changes pay.

In 2009, a Canadian dollar store did something that sounds like a small act of treason. Dollarama began selling things for $1.25, $1.50, and $2. The name stayed. The rule changed. For anyone trying to understand Bain Capital Private Equity, which had bought a majority stake five years earlier, those extra quarters are a useful place to begin.

Dollarama was already a growing business. By 2004, it had nearly 350 stores across six Canadian provinces. Bain did not invent its appeal. Larry Rossy and his team had built a retailer around inexpensive merchandise, direct importing, and a repeatable store format. The opportunity was to expand something customers already understood.

The acquisition was substantial: a 2006 securities filing records C$1,032.5 million paid for the business in November 2004. Financing included approximately C$374 million invested by Bain-managed funds through a mixture of securities, alongside bank and subordinated borrowing. This was ownership with financial obligations attached.

Then came more stores, a Montreal distribution centre in 2006, new price points, and a Toronto Stock Exchange listing in October 2009. Bain sold its remaining stake in 2011. Those events do not make every improvement Bain’s personal invention. They show the operating changes that accompanied its ownership.

The interesting shift was conceptual. A literal dollar ceiling limited the merchandise Dollarama could offer. Its own history explains that the higher prices expanded quality and variety. My reading: affordability was the promise worth preserving; one dollar was a mechanism that could change. The distinction is useful well beyond retail.

Boston supplies the glass. The investment thesis has to supply the view.

Bain Capital began in Boston in 1984. Its first fund raised $37 million. Mitt Romney and R. Coleman Andrews came from Bain & Company, the consultancy, and the early team brought the habits of strategy consulting into investing. The two firms are separate businesses, despite the shared surname and history.

Founding team member Geoff Rehnert described the starting point plainly in a FRONTLINE interview: “We were ex-consultants”. Their proposition was that understanding a company’s market and helping change its decisions could be more valuable when the adviser also owned part of the company.

Today, Bain’s private equity strategy includes a dedicated portfolio group of operating and strategy professionals. Its work spans consumer, industrial, healthcare, technology, and financial and business services companies. Managers get capital, but also people assigned to help with execution. Bain says those people can take interim operating roles when needed.

The people buying Bain’s investment proposition are usually far removed from a checkout. Its limited partners include pensions, foundations, endowments, financial institutions, family offices, and sovereign wealth funds. They commit capital to funds that acquire company stakes and seek eventual investment gains.

Portfolio companies occupy the other side of the relationship. Their executives need help with expansion, acquisitions, ownership transitions, or complicated separations from larger groups. A shopper buying protein powder or a company paying for building maintenance may encounter the portfolio without ever choosing Bain as a supplier.

Fund managers generally earn management fees and a share of investment profits under their agreements. That makes the vocabulary important. Money committed to a fund is investment capacity. It is different from the manager’s revenue, and different again from sales at companies the fund owns.

Total fund commitments. Not company revenue. Rounded figures.

That commitment split gives Bain’s alignment argument some substance: its related entities supplied the balance after roughly $11.8 billion came from outside investors. It does not establish future returns. It shows that the firm’s own circle has money exposed to the same fund.

Toys “R” Us supplies a harder test of the operating thesis. Bain, KKR, and Vornado acquired the retailer in 2005. In September 2017, it filed for Chapter 11. Its bankruptcy declaration described a combination of online competition, pressure from mass retailers, and a highly leveraged capital structure.

Approximately $400 million a year went to cash debt service. The declaration called that burden unsustainable in the competitive environment. Revenue had been declining over the previous five years. The financial structure consumed resources while the stores and online offer needed investment.

Here the first visible trouble was weakening trading; the financing made recovery harder. The filing supports that sequence, rather than a tidy explanation involving one mistake. The practical warning is straightforward: a plan to improve a business needs enough financial room to survive the period before improvement pays.

For an owner copying the method, the difficult part is separating a plausible idea from an affordable one. A wider assortment, a new warehouse, or a better website requires spending before the result is certain. The lesson of the two retailers is to examine the operating plan and the financing together.

The portfolio also reaches into less familiar places. In February 2025, a Bain-led consortium agreed to acquire Apleona from PAI Partners. The facilities manager had more than 40,000 employees and had reached €4 billion in 2024 revenue under its previous owner. Its agenda included acquisitions, building technology, and energy efficiency.

This is where Bain competes with global buyout firms such as KKR, Carlyle, and EQT. Capital alone offers little distinction. Bain’s stated case rests on industry knowledge, management partnerships, and operating resources. Those capabilities matter most where there is a specific business problem they can solve.

The scale keeps changing. Asia Fund VI closed at $10.5 billion in May 2026, with founder transitions and corporate carve-outs among the opportunities described. The small lesson remains portable: write down the operating change an investment requires. Test the customer promise. Budget for disappointment. And never mistake the ability to buy a company for proof that it can be improved.
